title: Early retirement: how much money you need
subtitle: Early retirement planning
openingQuestion: Hoa, 32, spends 15 million VND/month (180 million/year) and wants to retire early at 45, living entirely off her investment portfolio without working again. Using the 4%/year withdrawal rule common in the FIRE movement, roughly how much does Hoa need to accumulate before retiring?
openingOptions: 9 billion VND, with no need to apply any formula at all - just save as much as possible
About 4.5 billion VND - that is, 25 times annual spending
It can't be calculated at all, since early retirement always carries unpredictable financial risk
180 million VND - exactly one year of her current spending, with no multiplier applied
explanation: The 4% safe withdrawal rule is based on the Trinity Study: if you withdraw 4% of the portfolio's value each year (inflation-adjusted), the portfolio has a high probability of surviving 30 years without running out, since the remainder keeps earning a return. Working backward: the amount needed = annual spending x 25 (since 1/4% = 25). For Hoa spending 180 million/year, that's 180 million x 25 = 4.5 billion VND. This is a starting point for FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) calculations, not an absolute number - it needs adjusting for risk tolerance and retirement age.

diagram.label: = The capital needed to retire early

realWorldExample.description: Many FIRE communities in Vietnam (on forums and investing Facebook groups) apply a variant of the 25-times-spending rule, but usually adjust the withdrawal rate down to 3-3.5%/year instead of 4%, because retiring at 40-45 leaves a much longer post-retirement lifespan (40-50 years) than traditional retirement at 60 (20-25 years), calling for a larger safety margin.

quiz.question: What does the 4% rule mean in a retirement plan?
options: Contributing 4% of income to a pension fund each month
Keeping at most 4% of the total portfolio value in cash reserves once you fully retire
Investing so the portfolio grows at least 4% a year
Withdrawing 4% of the initial portfolio each year, inflation-adjusted
quiz.explanation: The 4% rule is a guideline for a safe withdrawal rate, based on historical market data - it isn't a requirement about returns or fees.

quiz.question: Why does someone aiming to retire at 40-45 (via FIRE) usually need a MORE CONSERVATIVE withdrawal rate than 4% (say, 3-3.5%)?
options: Because the time the portfolio has to sustain them is much longer
Because the market always drops sharply in the first 10 years of retirement
Because spending at age 40 is always far higher than at age 65
Because early retirees don't receive a BHXH pension
quiz.explanation: The 4% rule was originally tested over a roughly 30-year horizon. Retiring much earlier means the portfolio has to 'survive' much longer, so it needs a lower withdrawal rate or a bigger portfolio.

quiz.question: What core calculation underlies the FIRE movement?
options: The higher someone's income is, the correspondingly and automatically shorter their time to financial freedom becomes
The savings rate determines the number of years you need to work, not the income level
Just investing in exactly the right high-growth stocks is enough on its own to shorten the timeline needed
The number of years of work needed always equals your current age minus your desired early retirement age exactly
quiz.explanation: Saving 10% of income takes about 40 years; saving 50% takes about 17 years; 70% takes under 10 years. Notably, this figure doesn't depend on salary level, since spending is both what you save and what you have to sustain.

quiz.question: Why does an early retiree need a rate lower than 4%?
options: Because a young person's day-to-day living costs are always significantly higher than an older, retired person's
Because early retirees don't receive a social insurance pension
Because the portfolio has to last 40-50 years instead of the original 30-year assumption
Because the tax rate applied to early withdrawals is higher
quiz.explanation: The longer the horizon, the higher the chance of hitting a bad stretch of years, with no pension to cushion it. Many FIRE followers use 3-3.5%, meaning the savings target has to be about 15-30% higher.

quiz.question: What's the biggest risk that early-retirement plans often overlook in Vietnam?
options: The BHXH pension being fully and permanently cut off the moment you retire before the statutory retirement age
Being legally barred from returning to the labor market after retiring
Banks refusing to open an investment account for someone without a job
Medical and insurance costs once you're no longer covered by mandatory insurance
quiz.explanation: Retiring early means losing the health insurance an employer used to pay for, right at the start of 40 more years of health risk ahead. This is the line item FIRE spreadsheets often leave blank, and the one that can blow up the whole plan.

quiz.question: What does 'Barista FIRE' mean?
options: Leaving your main career but still working part-time to cover part of your spending
Saving enough money that you are certain you never have to work another single day for the rest of your life
Putting your entire life savings into opening a coffee shop business to generate passive income streams
Retiring early with full FIRE savings, then being forced back into full-time work once the money unexpectedly runs out
quiz.explanation: A more practical middle-ground option: the portfolio covers most of your spending, and a light part-time job covers the rest, usually along with health insurance. It lowers the savings target considerably compared to full FIRE.

keyTakeaways: The amount needed to retire is roughly annual spending x 25 (the 4%/year withdrawal rule)
The earlier you retire, the longer your portfolio has to sustain you, so you need a bigger safety margin (withdrawing 3-3.5% instead of 4%)
FIRE doesn't necessarily mean stopping work entirely - many people choose 'Barista FIRE' (part-time work) to ease the pressure of withdrawing capital
The lower your annual spending, the less you need to save - controlling spending matters just as much as accumulating wealth

practicePrompt.question: Phong, 30, wants to retire at 42 (FIRE) and expects to live entirely off his portfolio for the next 45-50 years. Why should he consider a 3-3.5% withdrawal rate instead of the traditional 4% rule?
options: Because the time his portfolio has to sustain him is much longer (45-50 years), so he needs a bigger safety margin
Because the 4% rule only applies to people over 60 and has no reference value at all for early retirees
Because a 3-3.5% withdrawal rate always guarantees a higher return than 4% in every market condition
There's nothing to consider, since the 4% rule is a fixed formula that applies identically to every retirement age
practicePrompt.explanation: The earlier you retire, the longer your portfolio has to sustain you, so you need a bigger safety margin (withdrawing 3-3.5% instead of 4%) to guard against running out of money over a much longer stretch.

summary.keyIdea: The amount needed to retire is roughly annual spending x 25 (the 4%/year withdrawal rule)
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: The earlier you retire, the longer your portfolio has to sustain you, so you need a bigger safety margin (withdrawing 3-3.5% instead of 4%)

application.title: Try the math right now
application.message: Take your total annual spending (a quick estimate is monthly spending x 12), multiply by 25 - that's the figure you'd need to retire under the 4% withdrawal rule.
application.secondary: Don't panic if the number looks huge - this is just a starting point for planning.

sections.text: 'Early retirement' sounds like a luxury reserved for the wealthy. But the FIRE movement (Financial Independence, Retire Early) shows it's a math problem you can actually calculate - and anyone who controls spending well and invests with discipline has a shot at it, even without necessarily retiring at 35.

The core question of early retirement isn't 'how much money do I have' but 'how much money do I need to never have to work for money again'. The answer depends entirely on one single variable: your annual spending, not the salary you used to earn.

The Trinity Study (US, 1990s) examined decades of stock and bond market history and found that if someone withdraws 4% of the portfolio's value in the first year of retirement, then adjusts that withdrawal for inflation each following year, the portfolio has a very high probability (over 90% across many historical scenarios) of not running out of money within 30 years. Working backward gives the formula: amount needed to save = annual spending x 25 (since 100% / 4% = 25).

items: Spending 10 million/month (120 million/year) -> need about 3 billion VND
Spending 20 million/month (240 million/year) -> need about 6 billion VND
Spending 30 million/month (360 million/year) -> need about 9 billion VND
Cutting spending by 1 million/month lowers the amount needed by about 300 million VND - this is why FIRE weighs optimizing spending as heavily as raising income

sections.label: A note on applying this in Vietnam
sections.text: The 4% rule was built from US market data with a highly diversified stock/bond portfolio and relatively stable inflation. Vietnam's market swings harder, inflation has had spiking periods (2008, 2011), and passive investment vehicles (index funds) are younger. Many people applying FIRE in Vietnam choose a more conservative withdrawal rate (3-3.5%/year) or add rental real estate to diversify their passive income sources.

Not everyone following FIRE stops working entirely. 'Fat FIRE' means retiring with high spending, a large portfolio, and a comfortable lifestyle maintained. 'Lean FIRE' means retiring with minimal spending, a much smaller portfolio, and accepting a simpler lifestyle. 'Barista FIRE' is a middle ground: saving enough to cover most living costs, then taking a light part-time job (which may have nothing to do with finance) to cover the rest, easing the pressure to withdraw capital quickly.

left.label: Traditional retirement (age 60)
left.text: Time the portfolio has to sustain you: 20-25 years. The safety margin can be smaller, and the 4% rule fits fairly directly.

right.label: FIRE early retirement (age 40-45)
right.text: Time the portfolio has to sustain you: 40-50 years. Needs a more conservative withdrawal rate (3-3.5%) or a larger portfolio to guard against a long stretch of bad market conditions.

lines: Early retirement isn't magic - it's a math problem involving your savings rate, your spending level, and disciplined investing time.
Even if you're not aiming to retire at 40, FIRE thinking (controlling spending, calculating a clear target number) still helps anyone plan more clearly for their own retirement age.
